title: Mirror Reflection
statement:
A square room has side length `p`, and all four of its walls are mirrors. Three of its corners hold receptors: receptor `0` sits in the southeast corner, receptor `1` in the northeast corner and receptor `2` in the northwest corner; the southwest corner has none.

A laser beam starts in the southwest corner and travels in a straight line until it hits the east wall at height `q` (measured up from receptor `0`). From there it keeps bouncing off the mirrors. Return the number of the receptor the beam reaches first. The inputs guarantee that the beam does reach one.
notes:
## Intuition

Following the beam bounce by bounce works (that is the brute force), but there is a neater view. Instead of reflecting the beam, reflect the **room**: tile the plane with mirrored copies of the square, and the beam becomes one straight line from the origin with slope `q / p`. It reaches a corner the first time both its x and y coordinates are multiples of `p`. Along the line, x = k·p gives y = k·q, so the first corner is at height y = lcm(p, q).

Which receptor that corner is depends only on parity. After crossing `roomsAcross = lcm / q` rooms sideways, the beam is on the west wall if that count is even and on the east wall if it is odd. After rising `roomsUp = lcm / p` rooms, it is at a top corner if that count is odd and a bottom corner if it is even. Both counts cannot be even, since the lcm is the smallest common multiple.

## Approach

1. Compute `a = gcd(p, q)` with Euclid's algorithm.
2. `lcm = (p / a) * q`, then `roomsAcross = lcm / q` and `roomsUp = lcm / p`.
3. If `roomsAcross` is even, the beam ends on the west wall at the top: receptor `2`.
4. Otherwise it is on the east wall: an even `roomsUp` means bottom (receptor `0`), odd means top (receptor `1`).

## Example 1, step by step

`p = 2`, `q = 1`. Euclid gives `a = 1`, so `lcm = 2`, `roomsAcross = 2` and `roomsUp = 1`. The beam crossed two rooms sideways, so it is back on the west wall, one room up, at the top: receptor `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(log p): Euclid's algorithm dominates.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Dividing `p` by the gcd before multiplying keeps the lcm small and exact.
- Check `roomsAcross` first: on the west wall the only receptor is `2`.
- When `q === p` the beam goes straight into the northeast corner; the formula gives `1` without a special case.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `a`, `b` | Euclid's working pair; `a` ends as gcd(p, q) |
| `rest` | remainder in one Euclid step |
| `lcm` | height at which the unfolded beam first hits a corner |
| `roomsAcross` | rooms crossed sideways (lcm / q) |
| `roomsUp` | rooms climbed upward (lcm / p) |

narration.2: Copy p and q into Euclid's working pair.
narration.4: Euclid's algorithm: repeat until the second number reaches zero.
narration.5: Take the remainder of a divided by b.
narration.7: ...and the remainder into b, which shrinks the pair but keeps its gcd.
narration.9: a is gcd(p, q); divide before multiplying to get the least common multiple exactly.
narration.10: How many room widths the unfolded beam crosses before it meets a corner.
narration.11: How many room heights it climbs on the way.
narration.12: An even number of widths puts the beam back on the west wall.
narration.13: The only receptor on the west wall is 2, in the top corner.
narration.15: On the east wall, an even number of heights means the bottom corner.
narration.18: Odd widths and odd heights: the northeast corner, receptor 1.
